paragraph: Bharata's heart leapt with joy for a moment, at the sight of his beloved city. He said that Ayodhya, with the green of its gardens, groves, white sands, with the wealth of its knowledge and riches, was the most beautiful city rivaling Indra's Amaravati.Entering it, he was puzzled at the unusual quiet of the city and he asked his charioteer, "Charioteer, tell me why a city renowned for its wealth, learning and beauty, where Vedic priests abound, where yagnas and yagas are always performed should look so joyless. Why do I not hear the clamor of people, the wheels of their chariots or the bustle of people on the streets?The gardens are so quiet, they seem seem to weep, deprived of their youthful visitors. Homes look deserted and yards are unclean.The trees in the gardens drooping seem to shed tears and not leaves.I hear neither beast nor bird.The air is no longer filled with the fragrance of incense and sandal. Why do the drums not boom and why is there no music? The stillness frightens me charioteer!Is it possible that all is not well with my kinsfolk?I see many inauspicious omens and I hear the cry of foxes that bode ill."
Situation/Problem_Faced: Upon entering Ayodhya, Bharata is struck by an unsettling and pervasive silence that contradicts the city's usual vibrancy. This unusual quiet, combined with the deserted appearance of homes and gardens, fills him with profound puzzlement, anxiety, and fear. He perceives the stillness as a bad omen and questions the well-being of his family.
Key_Teaching/Action_Taken: This passage powerfully conveys the psychological impact of an environment that deviates drastically from expectations. Bharata's detailed observations highlight how external cues can trigger intense internal distress, leading to a state of heightened alert and apprehension. His questioning serves as an attempt to find rational explanations for an emotionally unsettling situation.
Outcome/Resolution: Bharata's initial joy at seeing Ayodhya is quickly replaced by growing fear and anxiety due to the city's abnormal silence and deserted appearance. He vocalizes his deep concern and foreboding to his charioteer, expressing his dread that 'all is not well with my kinsfolk,' and noting ominous signs.
Brief_Summary_Spiritual: Bharata's initial joy gives way to deep 'Chinta' (anxiety) and 'Bhaya' (fear) as he encounters 'Ashubha Nimitta' (inauspicious omens) in the eerily silent Ayodhya. The absence of traditional auspicious sounds and the perceived sorrow of the city's nature indicate a disruption of 'Dharma' or cosmic order, inducing 'Vishada' (despondency) in Bharata, who instinctively senses a grave spiritual imbalance.
Brief_Summary_Psychological: Psychologically, Bharata experiences an acute onset of anxiety and fear triggered by a drastic perceptual incongruity between his expectation of a vibrant city and the observed desolation. His detailed observations reflect a hyper-vigilant state, and his anthropomorphic descriptions of the weeping gardens and shedding trees project his own low mood and sadness. His questions to the charioteer represent an attempt to externalize and process his profound internal distress and foreboding.
